For the next century and a half the family stayed in one corner of New York, the strip of Franklin and Clinton counties
between the Adirondacks and the Saint Lawrence.
It was cold, late-spring farm country, and its first wealth was timber: sawmills worked its rivers,
and the lumber went down toward the Saint Lawrence or, after the Northern Railroad came through Malone in 1850,
out by rail. Dana Hutchins kept a general store.
His son Allen Dana and his grandsons DeWitt and Frederick ran a lumber business at Fort Covington.
Six men of the Constable branch went to the Civil War.
As the forests were cut, the cleared land went to dairy farms, and the family’s work followed the country.
Not everyone stayed: Grace Southworth’s uncle Norman went out to the wheat country of the Palouse,
in eastern Washington, and after DeWitt Hutchins died in 1912 Grace went west too,
remarried, lived at Clarkston on the Snake River, and in 1949 was buried at Palouse,
in the same cemetery as her uncle. Doctor Clarence Hutchins, of the New York University class of 1911,
was health officer of Saranac from 1916 and of Dannemora from 1917.
His son DeWitt Allen came home from the Second World War and, about 1952, opened Elliott and Hutchins in Malone,
selling International Harvester tractors and machinery to the farms around.
